Pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) is a formal diagnostic category applied when serum hCG is above the discriminatory threshold (usually ≥1500–2000 mIU/mL) but no intra- or extrauterine pregnancy is visualized; it encompasses both early intrauterine pregnancies below detection limits and ectopic pregnancies, hence high plausibility. Ectopic pregnancy remains a critical, life-threatening diagnosis that must be actively ruled out—especially given its prevalence (~2% of pregnancies) and mortality risk—and is highly plausible in this context. Early spontaneous abortion (particularly missed or incomplete) may present with declining or plateauing hCG and absent sac; though less likely than early gestation, it warrants inclusion due to clinical impact. False-positive hCG is rare (<1% of positive tests) and usually associated with specific clinical contexts (e.g., perimenopause, malignancy, heterophilic antibodies); thus, it receives the lowest confidence. Diagnostic uncertainty (Shannon entropy) reflects moderate dispersion across plausible alternatives, consistent with an indeterminate early pregnancy evaluation."}
